extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners / attorneys practicing before the USPTO
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing ethical conduct of practitioners before the USPTO (accepting third‑party payments, conflicts, client communication, trust accounts, and discipline/probation procedures). Drawn from a USPTO Final Order interpreting 37 C.F.R. disciplinary rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain client's consent after full disclosure before accepting third‑party compensation (37 C.F.R. §10.68(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must obtain the client's consent, after full disclosure, before accepting compensation from someone other than the client for legal services to or for the client (cited as 37 C.F.R. §10.68(a)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To meet the “full disclosure” requirement the practitioner should inquire of both the third party and the client about the funds being collected and how much will be distributed to the practitioner. Example context: invention development companies or escrow arrangements where a third party pays the practitioner. Absent such inquiry, the practitioner may fail to recognize an impending disciplinary violation (e.g., hidden fee‑sharing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain consent after full disclosure when practitioner's judgment may be affected (37 C.F.R. §10.62(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may not accept employment without first receiving the client's consent after full disclosure in circumstances where the exercise of the practitioner's professional judgment will be, or reasonably may be, affected by the practitioner's own financial, business, property, or personal interests (cited as 37 C.F.R. §10.62(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a practitioner’s livelihood depends in some measure on regularly receiving referrals and compensation from a third party, the practitioner must have a frank and meaningful discussion fully informing the client of the actual and potential conflicts so the client can provide informed consent. Failure to do so risks disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely inform and adequately consult the client before taking action (37 C.F.R. §10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not take action on a client's behalf without the client's knowledge or consent and must inform the client on a timely basis of actions taken (cited as 37 C.F.R. §10.23(b)(6)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of the anti‑pattern include filing replies to Office Actions, filing or rescinding non‑publication requests, or deciding not to pursue an RCE without adequate client consultation or timely notice. Practitioners should consult and obtain client input prior to substantive filings and keep clients promptly informed of key decisions and filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a separate client trust account; avoid commingling (37 C.F.R. §§10.112(a),(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not commingle client funds with a law firm's operating funds; client funds should be maintained in a trust account separate from business/operating accounts (cited as 37 C.F.R. §§10.112(a),(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not deposit client checks for fees or filing costs into the operating account. Maintain proper trust accounting and promptly refund unearned fees held in the practitioner's possession. Failure to keep funds separate may result in discipline (example: placing an $895 client check in the operating account).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid impermissible sharing of legal fees with non‑practitioners; inquire to detect fee‑sharing (37 C.F.R. §10.48 and related guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner should avoid arrangements that effectively share legal fees with non‑practitioners; lack of inquiry into third‑party arrangements can result in impermissible fee‑sharing (see discussion of §10.48).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should ask both the third party and the client how funds are collected and distributed; if the third party is not a practitioner and retains funds that are not returned to the client, the arrangement may amount to sharing legal fees with a non‑practitioner in violation of the rules. Careful inquiry and documentation prevent inadvertent fee‑sharing violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inform clients about risks that third parties holding escrowed fees may not refund unearned amounts (37 C.F.R. §§10.40(a), 10.112(c)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners should communicate to clients that a non‑practitioner third party holding escrowed/unearned legal fees typically is not obligated by USPTO Disciplinary Rules to refund those fees, whereas the practitioner is obligated to refund unearned fees in the practitioner's possession (citing §§10.40(a) and 10.112(c)(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As part of full disclosure and informed consent, practitioners should explain escrow/refund risks to clients and advise how unearned fees will be handled so clients understand residual risks of third‑party escrow arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide copies of discipline orders to affected clients and file an affidavit of compliance (37 C.F.R. §11.20(a)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Office issues a Final Order imposing public discipline, the practitioner must provide copies of the Final Order to affected clients within specified timeframes and file an affidavit confirming compliance (page requires providing copies within 30 days and filing an affidavit within 45 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comply with the stated deadlines and retain proof of service. This is a mandatory post‑discipline compliance obligation (example: provide Final Order to Mr. L. and Mr. M. within 30 days and file an affidavit within 45 days).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation and stayed suspension enforcement procedure (Order to Show Cause; 15‑day response; possible lifting of stay and suspension)
rubrics_metrics.description: A stayed suspension may be maintained during a probationary period; if the OED Director believes the practitioner failed to comply with the Final Order or any Disciplinary Rule during probation, the Director will issue an Order to Show Cause, send it to the practitioner's last address, and grant 15 days to respond. If noncompliance persists, the OED Director may deliver the record to the USPTO Director and request lifting the stay and immediate suspension for up to six months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the enforcement steps, timelines, and potential outcomes for probation violations: issuance of Order to Show Cause, 15‑day response window, evidentiary submission to USPTO Director, and possible immediate suspension up to six months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and notice of public discipline (37 C.F.R. §11.59)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public discipline will be published: the OED Director shall publish the Final Order in the OED Reading Room, publish notices (e.g., Notice of Stayed Suspension) in the Official Gazette, and give notice of public discipline and reasons to state disciplinary agencies, courts where the practitioner is admitted, and the public (cited as 37 C.F.R. §11.59).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should expect public dissemination of discipline and that the record may be considered in future proceedings as an aggravating factor or to rebut statements by the practitioner. The Final Order will be posted electronically and otherwise disseminated as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended client‑communication and practice management practices to avoid discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Best practices shown by the respondent's corrective measures: send all Office correspondence to the client, discuss correspondence by phone or e‑mail, maintain a separate trust account for client funds, and cease accepting problematic third‑party referrals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt proactive communication (forward Office notices, timely consult on responses/filings), sound trust accounting, and avoid routine referral arrangements that create conflicts. These practices reduce risk of the types of violations found in the Final Order.
